clue.text: In his panic, he saw life as a used car dump

definitions.text: In his panic, he saw life as a used car dump

parts.words: In his panic, he saw life as a used car dump
parts.note: points to the Spanish dramatist who co-founded the Panic movement and wrote the play The Car Cemetery, a nightmarish vision set in a scrapyard

explanation.surface: A frightened man has a bleak vision of existence as a scrapyard of old cars.
explanation.walkthrough: Panic is not fear here but the Panic Movement of avant-garde theatre; the car dump is the setting of the dramatist's play The Car Cemetery.
explanation.definitionFit: Fernando Arrabal, Spanish-born playwright, founded the Panic Movement and wrote Le Cimetière des voitures, a play set among wrecked cars.

clue.text: Called a bearer of tidings by Philip MacDonald

definitions.text: Called a bearer of tidings by Philip MacDonald

parts.words: Called a bearer of tidings by Philip MacDonald
parts.note: points to the forename of the man in the title of MacDonald's mystery novel, whose surname is Messenger, a bearer of tidings

explanation.surface: A novelist names someone as the person who brings the news.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip MacDonald wrote The List of Adrian Messenger; the character's surname means a bearer of tidings, and 'called' asks for his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Philip MacDonald's thriller The List of Adrian Messenger bears this forename.

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
a perch, like a rod, is an old measure of length, also called a pole

explanation.surface: An odd fish of a perch belongs to a man called Mortimer.
explanation.walkthrough: John Mortimer created the barrister Horace Rumpole of the Bailey. 'Perch' suggests the fish, but here it is the land measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace Rumpole is the Old Bailey barrister invented by the writer John Mortimer.

parts.note: the military rank held by Conan Doyle's boastful Napoleonic hussar, Etienne Gerard, whose stories carry the rank in their titles

explanation.surface: Someone is placed on a level with a famous character from Conan Doyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ranks with' seems to mean 'equals', but it asks for the officer's rank that is paired with Gerard's name in Conan Doyle's Exploits of Brigadier Gerard.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's Napoleonic hussar is known by his military title, an army officer rank above colonel.

parts.note: the married name of the youngest Bennet sister in Pride and Prejudice, who elopes with the officer Wickham

explanation.walkthrough: In Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice the flighty youngest sister runs off with George Wickham and becomes his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's youngest Bennet daughter marries the officer George Wickham after their elopement.

clue.text: Clue ego ", perhaps, for pastoral poem

indicators.note: perhaps says these letters may stand for something else, so they are rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: A clue made from the word ego might suggest a country poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray quotation mark is a printing glitch; 'perhaps' tells us to rearrange CLUE EGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's Eclogues are the classic short pastoral poems in which shepherds converse.

indicators.note: including means the letters sought are held within the words fine art

explanation.surface: Fine art, at its best, contains a talent for music.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a good ear for music has a natural talent for picking out pitch and melody.

clue.text: Frederic Raphael observed more than one to love

definitions.text: Frederic Raphael observed more than one to love

parts.words: Frederic Raphael observed more than one to love
parts.note: the clue asks for the singular of the plural word in that title

explanation.surface: A writer noticed that a person had more than one lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More than one to love' reads as rivals in love, but it describes the plural in Raphael's title The Limits of Love; the answer is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederic Raphael's first big novel was The Limits of Love, and one of those boundaries is the singular word.

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken aloud and a near-identical name is heard

parts.note: a gardener is someone hired to help with work outdoors

explanation.surface: The fictional lawyer gets assistance from someone outside his office.
explanation.walkthrough: Erle Stanley Gardner created the lawyer Perry Mason; 'Perry Mason's' stands for his author, as in 'Perry Mason's man'.
explanation.definitionFit: The courtroom stories of Perry Mason were written by the American author Erle Stanley Gardner.

clue.text: "The House of Lords is a perfect home" (Baroness Stocks)

definitions.text: "The House of Lords is a perfect home" (Baroness Stocks)

parts.words: "The House of Lords is a perfect home" (Baroness Stocks)
parts.note: the quotation has a word missing before home; Mary Stocks called the Lords a perfect retirement home for the elderly

explanation.surface: A peeress remarks that the House of Lords is the ideal place to live.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is printed with its key word missing: Baroness Stocks said the House of Lords was 'a perfect eventide home', a British phrase for an old people's home.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventide means evening, the close of day, and figuratively old age, as in the Salvation Army's homes for the elderly.

definitions.meaning: the rest is what is left over
a book that a publisher sells off cheaply because it has not sold

explanation.surface: The remaining copies of a book have been cut in price.
explanation.definitionFit: What is left over is the remainder, and unsold stock sold off cheaply by a publisher is said to be remaindered.

definitions.meaning: a system of dots and dashes for sending messages
the detective whose cases Colin Dexter wrote, the inspector watched by the writer

explanation.surface: A crime novelist notices a secret cipher in use.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Dexter's Oxford detective shares his surname with Samuel Morse's telegraph code.
explanation.definitionFit: The telegraph code of dots and dashes and Colin Dexter's Oxford police inspector share the name.

clue.text: Fragrance to capital, as Moravia might say

definitions.text: to capital, as Moravia might say
definitions.meaning: the Italian novelist Alberto Moravia would say 'to Rome' in his own language as two words

explanation.surface: A scent goes to the city, in the words of an Italian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: In Italian, 'a Roma' means 'to Rome', and Rome is the capital; Alberto Moravia was a Roman novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasant smell, such as coffee's, is a fragrance or scent.

clue.text: John Bulls'" creator who had a letter from Pope

definitions.meaning: the Scottish physician and satirist who invented John Bull, the figure for England, in his 1712 pamphlets

definitions.text: who had a letter from Pope
definitions.meaning: Alexander Pope addressed his verse Epistle to this doctor friend

explanation.surface: The man who invented John Bull once received correspondence from the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope' is not the pontiff but Alexander Pope, whose Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot is a verse letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr John Arbuthnot created John Bull in his History of John Bull and received Pope's verse Epistle.

parts.note: Ben Jonson's comedy named after a London fair held on a saint's day at Smithfield

explanation.surface: Ben Jonson behaves honestly and plays by the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair play' reads as sportsmanship, but it is a play about a fair: Jonson's comedy Bartholomew Fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Bartholomew Fair, Ben Jonson's 1614 comedy, is set at London's annual Smithfield fair on St Bartholomew's day.

clue.text: Drama about city maintenance (as in Canaletto)?

definitions.text: Drama about city maintenance (as in Canaletto)?

parts.words: Drama about city maintenance (as in Canaletto)?
parts.note: Thomas Otway's tragedy whose title says the Italian city has been kept safe, the way a Canaletto painting keeps its image

explanation.surface: A play tells of the upkeep of a city as painted by Canaletto.
explanation.walkthrough: Otway's 1682 tragedy Venice Preserv'd has a title that could describe Canaletto's paintings of Venice preserving the city on canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Otway's Restoration tragedy Venice Preserv'd concerns a plot against the Venetian state.

definitions.meaning: a muscle that bends the knee, the long thigh muscle
the slum landlord in George Bernard Shaw's play Widowers' Houses

explanation.surface: A character in Shaw who owns property has a muscle that bends the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest muscle in the body crosses the thigh to bend the knee; Shaw gave its name to the slum owner in Widowers' Houses.

clue.text: Holy man (a Zealot perhaps) produces tragic ode

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint
Simon the Zealot was one of the twelve apostles

explanation.surface: A religious fanatic writes a sorrowful poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zealot' looks like a general fanatic, but it is the apostle Simon the Zealot.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek tragedy a stasimon is a choral song sung by the chorus standing in place between episodes.

parts.note: the title of the historical novel by Evelyn Anthony about a foreign wife, read as Mark Antony's partner

explanation.surface: Mark Antony has a foreign wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony suggests Mark Antony and his Egyptian queen, but the reference is to the novelist Evelyn Anthony's book The French Bride.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride from France is a foreign spouse, the title of a novel by Evelyn Anthony.

clue.text: "What can sots, or slaves, or cowards?" (Pope)

definitions.text: "What can sots, or slaves, or cowards?" (Pope)

parts.words: "What can sots, or slaves, or cowards?" (Pope)
parts.note: the line from Pope's Essay on Man is printed with its verb missing after 'can'; the full line ends with all the blood of all the Howards

explanation.surface: Pope asks what drunkards, slaves and cowards are capable of.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation lacks its verb: Pope wrote 'What can ennoble sots, or slaves, or cowards? / Alas! not all the blood of all the Howards.'
explanation.definitionFit: To ennoble is to make noble or raise to the peerage, which Pope says birth alone cannot do for the base.

definitions.meaning: the first noun in the title of Edward Gibbon's history of the Roman Empire's ... and fall

explanation.surface: Someone turns down a section of Gibbon's history.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn down politely is to decline; Gibbon's history is The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.

parts.note: Higgins's early thriller The ... Lover names where its title character comes from, the Greek island of Crete

explanation.surface: Where a thriller writer's romantic partner comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Higgins wrote The Cretan Lover; the 'origin' is the adjective of place in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Crete is Cretan, the place of origin in the Higgins novel's title.

clue.text: Russell Thorndyke's doctor has foot with fused digits

parts.note: Doctor Syn is the smuggling vicar in Russell Thorndike's novels
a dactyl is a metrical foot of one long and two short syllables

explanation.surface: A fictional doctor has a foot whose toes are joined together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' suggests a limb, but it is the verse foot. Doctor Syn is Russell Thorndike's smuggler-parson of Romney Marsh.
explanation.definitionFit: A syndactyl animal or person has webbed or joined fingers or toes.

definitions.meaning: the Titan who fought against Zeus and was condemned to hold up the sky
an American intercontinental ballistic missile shared the Titan's name

explanation.surface: A rebellious giant completely lost his temper.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titan who warred on Zeus was made to bear the heavens; an American ICBM of the 1950s bore his name.

definitions.meaning: the gold figure given as the American film award
Wilde, author of The Ballad of Reading Gaol, by his first name

explanation.surface: A film award goes to someone who sings ballads in a reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading is the English town, its gaol the subject of Oscar Wilde's ballad, not the act of reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award trophy is nicknamed this, and Oscar Wilde wrote The Ballad of Reading Gaol.

clue.text: Serving girl where diners are set apart

definitions.text: Serving girl where diners are set apart

parts.words: Serving girl where diners are set apart
parts.note: the waitress in Terence Rattigan's play Separate Tables, set in a hotel dining room where guests eat at their own tables

explanation.surface: A waitress works in a restaurant where customers are kept apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where diners are set apart' describes Rattigan's Separate Tables, whose hotel waitress is named Mabel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Rattigan's Separate Tables the waitress at the Beauregard Hotel bears this name.

clue.text: Sassoon, for example, strangely omits rime

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of the following words are arranged oddly into a new word

explanation.surface: Sassoon's poems oddly leave out rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: Siegfried Sassoon is thought of as a poet, so 'rime' looks apt, but here he is the author of Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man.
explanation.definitionFit: Siegfried Sassoon wrote autobiographical books such as Memoirs of an Infantry Officer, making him a writer of personal recollections.

definitions.meaning: Pope's Essay on ... takes humankind as its subject
the quoted line at 18 comes from Pope's Essay on ..., named here by its last word

explanation.surface: The topic of an essay is the origin of another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves point to Pope's An Essay on Man: its subject, and the poem from which the quotation at 18 down is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope's philosophical poem An Essay on Man takes humankind as its subject and supplies the quotation at 18.

clue.text: Moody Dane of The Four Temperaments

definitions.text: Moody Dane of The Four Temperaments

parts.words: Moody Dane of The Four Temperaments
parts.note: the Danish composer whose Second Symphony, The Four Temperaments, portrays four contrasting moods

explanation.surface: A temperamental Dane appears in a work about four temperaments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moody Dane' suggests Hamlet, but this Dane wrote a symphony about moods: Carl Nielsen's Symphony No 2.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Nielsen, Denmark's leading composer, wrote the symphony The Four Temperaments depicting four humours.

parts.note: points to Synge's comedy The Playboy of the ... World, asking for the word that qualifies World in its title

explanation.surface: A play about a playboy in his own world.
explanation.walkthrough: J M Synge's The Playboy of the Western World: the missing word describes the world in the playboy's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Synge's play is The Playboy of the Western World, set in the west of Ireland.
